newsitem.title: GREECE: FEATURE - Greece determined to qualify for EMU by 2001.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Greece determined to qualify for EMU by 2001.

text.p: Greece, the only European Union country in the Balkans, is focusing its economic policies on meeting the qualifying targets for European monetary union by 2001.

"Our aim is to put Greece on a European course, which means meeting the economic goals set out in the budget," Prime Minister Costas Simitis said recently. "We can achieve convergence on condition that we believe in it."
Analysts think the task is realistic given the national consensus on the issue, but are quick to add that more painful austerity measures may be required than the government currently envisages.

"Greece will be a member of the EMU (Economic and Monetary Union) in 2001," said Panos Panayiotopoulos, head of the money market and forex desk at the private Alpha Credit bank. "There is consensus among politicians, businessmen and others that Greece has no other option."
CRITERIA
Three years ago Greece agreed with the European Commission to implement an ambitious five-year convergence plan aimed at joining the single currency.

The plan aimed to bring the general government budget deficit down to 10.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the January to December 1995 fiscal year, 7.6 percent in 1996 and 4.2 percent in 1997.

Greece has overshot the targets so far, but bigger deficits were offset by higher-than-expected economic growth and surpluses from social security funds, hospitals and local authorities. The real deficits were therefore on target.
Budget deficits in 1995 and 1996 were 9.1 percent of GDP and 7.4 percent respectively. Government projections for 1997 aim to meet the 4.2 percent target as proposed by the commission in 1994.

The EMU convergence plan for Greece was formulated at a time when surpluses of social security funds from the restructuring of the pensions system in the early 1990s had not been expected. The surpluses were incorporated into the budget starting in 1995.
SUPPLEMENTARY BUDGET POSSIBLE

Tax revenues have been sluggish in the first two months of 1997, lagging behind the 14.6 percent ordinary budget target, prompting market speculation of a supplementary budget in the summer. Spending figures are not yet available.
The ordinary budget is defined as the central government budget excluding the investment budget.

"A supplementary budget looks more likely now than it did a month ago," said George Georgiou, deputy general manager at Bayerische Vereinsbank, Athens. "However it will be a political decision contingent on the EMU timetable."
PRIVATISATION COULD BOOST REVENUES AND AVOID SOCIAL UNREST

Speeding up the implementation of the government's privatisation agenda could bring in badly needed revenues and make up for any shortfalls in the short term. It would also allow the government to avoid social unrest that a supplementary budget may cause if it slashed spending, some bankers said.

Privatisation receipts amounted to 31 billion drachmas ($117.2 million) in 1996 and the government hopes to raise more money by floating an unspecified stake in telecommunications company OTE and 10 percent of state Public Petroleum Corporation (DEP) by end-97.
The government floated about eight percent of OTE in April 1996.
Economy ministry officials are considering the privatisation of the profitable duty free shops and selling a 49 percent in the Olympic Catering company this year through the Athens bourse.

Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou has said the state will try once again to sell the Bank of Crete in the next few months. A previous attempt earlier this year failed when the sole bidder, the private Bank of Piraeus, withdrew.
PROSPECTS IMPROVING BUT GAP TO EUROPEAN MAINSTREAM HUGE

Another strong card is faster economic growth. Greece has revised its 1997 GDP growth forecast to 3.5 percent from an initial 3.3 percent on estimates of stronger investment spending by the private and public sectors.
"I am optimistic about the course of the economy because there are the ingredients that can sustain satisfactory GDP growth rates in the future," said Georgiou.
Yet, despite improvements in inflation, interest rates and fiscal balances, Greece failed to meet a single Maastricht criterion at the end of 1996, putting it at the end of the queue for EMU.

February consumer price inflation eased to 6.6 percent year-on-year from 6.8 percent in January and is expected to drop to around 6.2-6.3 percent in March. EU-harmonised inflation data put Greek inflation at 6.6 percent in January.
But February core consumer price inflation excluding volatile food and energy prices rose to 7.9 percent from 7.5 percent in January, showing the improvement was fragile, bankers said.

"A good deal of the disinflation can be explained by lower international gasoline prices and good weather conditions which have helped suppress prices of fruit and fresh vegetables," said a senior dealer at a foreign bank.

After-tax yields on three-year fixed coupon bonds due in 2000 hover below the 10 percent mark in the secondary market and after-tax rates on 12-month T-bills have fallen to about 9.6 percent from a tax-free 11.2 percent at end-December 1996.
TIES TO BALKANS ARE IMPORTANT FACTOR FOR GREEK ECONOMY
Chaos in Albania, the economic crisis in Bulgaria and Romania and the still unsettled situation in former Yugoslavia could hit Greek firms.

"One has to take into consideration the trade-off between short-term costs and long-term benefits when evaluating Greek investments in these countries," said Andonis Ioannidis, privatisation consultant at Vakakis International.
The bulk of Greek investment is from light industrial firms seeking to exploit the comparative advantage of cheap labour offered by these countries, he said.

"These firms might have to digest some losses in the short run but the medium to long-term potential justifies them," he added. "The wave of the future will be infrastructure projects financed by international organisations such as the EBRD (European Bank of Reconstruction and Development) and Greek firms have to be there."
Greece also stands to gain from the troubles of its neighbours by becoming the base for international companies and organisations doing business in the Balkans, added Ioannidis.
OLD RIVALRY WITH TURKEY IS CONSTANT SOURCE OF CONCERN
Some bankers voice concern over the Greek-Turkish rivalry that has threatened at times to escalate into an armed conflict.
"I am not worried about the situation in other Balkan countries where I see some long-term benefits for Greek companies but this is not so when it comes to Turkey," said Georgiou.
Other bankers agreed, noting that periodic tension between Greece and Turkey had prompted some foreign investors to demand a larger risk premium for Greek debt than usual.
